sentences.text: Tupandactylus is a genus of pterodactyloid tapejarid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous Crato Formation of Brazil.
This animal is notable for a large cranial crest made of both bone and soft tissue fibers, likely keratin.
The species T. imperator had a large, rounded crest, while T. navigans had a tall, vertical crest.
The first five dorsal vertebrae of Tupandactylus are fused into a notarium, a structure also found in some other pterosaurs and birds.
The sternum of Tupandactylus was wide and roughly square.
The radius and ulna of Tupandactylus were straight and lightly built.
Rhamphotheca, or beaks, are known from multiple Tupandactylus specimens.
The species T. navigans appeared in the 1999 TV series Walking with Dinosaurs, but it was not formally described and named until 2003.
A well-preserved fossil of T. imperator had pigment cells with forms similar to modern birds, more complex than those previously known from other pterosaurs.
A specimen of T. imperator suggests the presence of Stage IIIa feathers, indicating complex filament structures in pterosaurs.
The genus Tupandactylus was established by Kellner and Campos in 2007.
The species T. imperator was originally described by Campos and Kellner in 1997 as a species of Tapejara, but later research indicated it was a separate genus.
The holotype specimen, a skull and partial lower jaw, was found in the Crato Formation and dates to about 112 million years ago at the Aptian-Albian boundary.
Tupandactylus is based on material MCT 1622-R, an almost complete skull found in the Santana Formation.

Examination of specimen GP/2E 9266 suggests Tupandactylus was capable of flight but spent much time on the ground due to its large crest, long forelimbs, and long neck, taking only short flights possibly to escape predators.
The mandible of the well-preserved T. imperator skull is associated with plant material, which may represent a taphonomic phenomenon or tentative evidence of herbivory.
A research team suggested that the thin crest on Tupandactylus's head acted as a sensory organ similar to a modern flight computer to help control agility.
Researchers proposed that Tupandactylus could use its wings like boat sails to catch light breezes and move like a catamaran.
The genus Tupandactylus includes the species T. imperator and T. navigans.
Both T. navigans and T. imperator are found within the tribe Tapejarini, which is within the larger group Tapejaridae.
Tupandactylus belongs to the parent group Tapejaridae.
Ingridia is a synonym of Tupandactylus, proposed by Unwin and Martill in 2007.
Researchers Kellner and Campos proposed the new genus Tupandactylus in 2006 because they found that species previously assigned to Tapejara were anatomically distinct.
Tupandactylus lived during the Early Cretaceous.
Tupandactylus lived during the Aptian stage, between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago.
While two species are currently recognized, it has been suggested that there may be only a single, highly sexually dimorphic species, though this requires further testing.

There was a taxonomic debate where Unwin and Martill proposed the genus name "Ingridia" for both species, but Campos and Kellner's proposed name "Tupandactylus" was ultimately accepted because their publication preceded the book by Unwin and Martill.
The common origin of pterosaur feathers and bird feathers remains controversial.
Frey, Martill, and Buchy argued in 2003 that the large head crest significantly impacted aerodynamics and that adaptations to counteract it were absent.
It is debated whether Tupandactylus could sail using its wings, as some studies suggest tapejarids had short wings adapted for terrestrial life and climbing trees rather than sailing.
There is no evidence supporting an aerodynamic function for the crest, and some researchers argue that the original proponent of this idea ignored recent aerodynamic studies.
